notes:
Here are my research notes on 2 Samuel 4. The older commentators mostly agree on what the chapter means. Where they disagree, it's between individual writers, not between denominations, and I found no material from particular Protestant traditions, Catholic or Orthodox sites, or popular modern movements that reads this chapter differently.

---

**v. 1**
- **Guzik:** Ish-bosheth knew he was finished once the man who had put him on the throne was dead. He was weak because he relied on a man. When Ishbosheth heard that the man who put and propped him on the throne was dead, he knew that his day was almost over. He trusted in man to gain his position, so when the man was gone, he knew his position would be soon gone. Ishbosheth was weak because he trusted in man. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-4/
- **Precept Austin:** The Hebrew literally says "his hands were feeble." The page says Ish-bosheth was like his father: he never learned to turn to the Lord in a crisis. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-4-commentary
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The news hit him twice over. His main support was dead, and Abner had also been secretly negotiating with David. Israel's "trouble" was uncertainty more than fear, because Abner's murder made people suspect David. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Matthew Henry (quoted by Precept Austin):** When difficulties discourage us instead of spurring us on, we put both our heavenly crowns and our earthly lives at risk. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-4-commentary

**v. 2**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The "bands" were light-armed raiding troops. Calling Ish-bosheth only "Saul's son" sounds slightly contemptuous. The bands mentioned were light-armed troops, used in forays, such as that mentioned in 2 Samuel 3:22. Their captains would be men of importance with Ishbosheth, who is here described somewhat contemptuously, not as king, nor by his own name, but as "Saul's son." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Clarke:** The Latin Vulgate and the Syriac call them "captains of banditti" (bandits). Such persons would be well qualified for the bloody work they did later. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Guzik:** They were Benjaminites, from Saul's own tribe, so it was fellow Benjaminites who murdered Ishbosheth. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-4/

**vv. 2–3 (Beeroth and Gittaim): who the brothers were and why they fled**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Beeroth was one of the four Gibeonite towns (Joshua 9:17). It thinks Saul's attack on the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1–2) caused the flight, so it was thus remarkable that the destruction of Saul's dynasty was the work of the Gibeonites of Beeroth. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Barnes:** If the flight happened during Saul's attack on the Gibeonites, the brothers may have killed Saul's son out of revenge for their people. The fact of their being reckoned as Benjamites is quite compatible with their being Canaanites by blood. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-3.htm
- **Coffman:** Goes further: "These were not Israelites, but Amorites or Canaanites, whose father was from a Gibeonite city; they were mercenaries in Ishbosheth's army." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-samuel-4.html
- **A different explanation:**
  - Gill: the Beerothites fled after Saul died, when many Israelites abandoned their towns to the Philistines (1 Samuel 31:7). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-3.htm
  - Geneva Study Bible: they fled "for fear of the Philistines." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-3.htm
- **Lange:** Mentions the revenge theory but cautions we know nothing certainly about it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Where Gittaim was:** Unclear. Keil and Delitzsch say it is never mentioned again, and has not yet been discovered. Clarke thought it was probably Gath. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-3.htm ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Ellicott:** "To this day" suggests the writer lived not long after these events. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-3.htm

**v. 4 (Mephibosheth)**
- **Why this verse is here:**
  - Barnes: partly to show that once Ish-bosheth died, the cause of Saul's house became hopeless, and partly to prepare for Mephibosheth's later appearances (2 Samuel 9; 16; 19). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-4.htm
  - Matthew Poole: it explains what encouraged the murderers. With Ish-bosheth gone, only a lame child would be left, so they expected David to reward them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-4.htm
- **His age:** Guzik says he was by now only 12 years old – and he was lame. He was weak because of his age and because of an injury that came from the hand of another. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-4/
- **His name:** Cambridge Bible: he is called Merib-baal in 1 Chronicles 8:34 and 9:40. Bosheth (="shame") has been substituted for the detested name of Baal, as in the name Ish-bosheth for Esh-baal. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-4.htm
- **Application (Pulpit Commentary sermon notes):** Lifelong suffering calls for trusting resignation. If active service of God be impossible, the service of patient endurance is not, and may be equally acceptable and useful. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Typology (Bible Hub study article, a modern evangelical piece):** Mephibosheth's lameness points ahead to David's grace in chapter 9 and to Christ's welcome of the lame (Luke 14:21–23). — https://biblehub.com/q/Significance_of_Mephibosheth_s_disability.htm

**v. 5**
- **Guzik:** A midday siesta was normal there, but having no guards shows carelessness. He quotes Trapp: "He dieth therefore in his sloth, who had lived slothfully all his days." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-4/
- **Matthew Henry:** When we lie down to sleep, we are not sure that we may not sleep the sleep of death before we awake; nor do we know from what hand the death-blow may come. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-4.htm

**v. 6 (the "wheat" ruse, and a known difference between ancient texts)**
- **The usual reading:** The brothers came on the excuse of collecting wheat, probably rations for their soldiers, who were paid in grain.
  - Poole: on that excuse they were let in and went from room to room to where the king lay. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-6.htm
  - Clarke: this natural explanation renders unnecessary all the emendations of Houbigant and others. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/2-samuel/4-6.html
- **The Greek Septuagint version:** It says instead that the woman guarding the door fell asleep while cleaning wheat, so the brothers slipped in unnoticed. Translations split here: the ESV puts this in a footnote, and the NLT and RSV put it in the main text. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/esv/2sa/4/1/ ; https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kja/2-samuel/4-6.html
- **Commentators disagree on which reading is original:**
  - Cambridge Bible: the Greek reading gives a clear straightforward narrative, and certainly seems preferable to the repetitions of the present Hebrew text. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-6.htm
  - Keil and Delitzsch: the doorkeeper line in the Vulgate is only an added note, since none of the other ancient translators found it in their text. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-6.htm
  - Pulpit Commentary: the text is confused, the other versions don't fully clear it up, and we must wait for better evidence. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Catholic translation:** The Douay-Rheims, translated from the Vulgate, includes the doorkeeper at the end of v. 5. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/2-samuel/4-5.html

**v. 7**
- **Why the murder is told twice (vv. 6 and 7):**
  - Barnes calls the repetition hard to account for.
  - Cambridge Bible: the first account is brief, and the second adds fuller details.
  - Keil and Delitzsch quote Königsfeldt: "The Hebrews often repeat in this way, for the purpose of adding something fresh, as for example, in this instance, their carrying off the head."
  - All three: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-6.htm
- **Guzik:** Cutting off the head was central to the plan, as proof for David. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-4/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The "bed" was probably a divan (a raised couch along the wall) in a private room. The "plain" they fled through was the Arabah, the Jordan valley. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html

**v. 8**
- **Guzik, quoting Joyce Baldwin:** The brothers presented themselves as God's instruments. Baldwin: "Their claim, The Lord has avenged my lord the king, was presuming on God's approval of their deed, as though they had acted on the Lord's express orders." Also, David did not think of Saul as his enemy. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-4/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Ish-bosheth himself had never tried to kill David. The religious language was ordinary in that culture, but here it was meant to win over a genuinely devout king. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html

**v. 9**
- **Matthew Henry:** David backed his sentence with an oath so nobody would plead for the criminals. It also showed he depended on God for the throne and would not be beholden to any man to help him to it by any indirect or unlawful practices. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_004.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary:**
  - "Redeemed" here simply means "delivered" from Saul's persecution, not spiritual redemption of the soul. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/4.htm
  - David uses the same oath in 1 Kings 1:29, which suggests he used it throughout his reign. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/4.htm
  - The sermon section still applies it to Christ as Redeemer. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Precept Austin:** David consistently left God to deal with whoever stood in his way, so he could have no part in this murder even though it cleared his path to the throne. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-4-commentary

**v. 10**
- **Matthew Henry:** David cites a precedent, the Amalekite messenger he executed at Ziklag (2 Samuel 1). — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_004.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The sense is "that was the reward I gave him for his tidings." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html

**v. 11**
- **Matthew Henry:** David treats Ish-bosheth as an honest man, even though he had caused David a great deal of trouble. Killing him at home and in bed made the crime worse. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_004.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Ish-bosheth was probably weak rather than wicked. "Righteous" means he was guiltless toward Rechab and Baanah. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-4.html
- **Guzik, quoting G. Campbell Morgan:** No servant of His can ever consent to do evil that good may come. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-4/

**v. 12**
- **Purpose of the punishment:**
  - Barnes: the display was meant to deter others and to show Israel that David had no part in the murder.
  - Gill: the hands struck the blow and the feet ran with the head, which the Jews call "measure for measure."
  - Both: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-12.htm
- **What was hung up is disputed:**
  - Gill (following the early church writer Theodoret): the mutilated bodies. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-12.htm
  - Matthew Henry: only the hands and feet, because the Law forbade displaying whole bodies. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/4-12.html
- **Was it lawful?**
  - Pulpit Commentary: David was violating the spirit of the Mosaic Law (Deuteronomy 21:23), though it should not be judged harshly given the customs of the time. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/4-12.htm
  - Matthew Henry: by contrast, the men were executed "according to law." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/4-12.html
- **Burial:** Ellicott says Ish-bosheth's head was buried with honour in the tomb of his chief supporter, Abner. — https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/4-12.htm
- **Keil and Delitzsch (quoted by Guzik):** David acted out of real horror at the crime and to keep his conscience void of offense towards God and towards man. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-4/

---

**What I couldn't find:**
- **Denominational differences:** The real disagreements are between individual commentators: the Greek vs Hebrew wording in v. 6, the brothers' motive in vv. 2–3, and what was hung up in v. 12 and whether it was lawful.
- **Modern scholarship:** I didn't reach the NET Bible notes or any Bible Odyssey article.
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I didn't reach New Advent, Catholic.com or OCA. The only Catholic material is the Douay-Rheims wording in v. 5.
- **Prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on this chapter.
